commentary.heading: Wall Street bounces back from its worst week since April 2025
commentary.body: US shares fell sharply last week as investors dumped AI and chip stocks after the Democrats won both houses of Congress: the Nasdaq lost 3.4% and the S&P 500 2.7%. Friday steadied things, helped by a much stronger-than-expected jobs report (165,000 new jobs against about 65,000 forecast, with unemployment down to 4.1%). On Monday the S&P 500 jumped 2.35% to 7,550, its best day since April, and the Nasdaq rose 2.7% as chipmakers rebounded and analysts called the AI sell-off overdone. Brent crude fell about 6% to around US$92 after President Trump played down the chance of new strikes on Iran, easing inflation worries. Nvidia bucked the rally, falling about 4% on a board investigation into whether a foreign intelligence effort targeted its chief executive.

commentary.heading: ASX: flat Monday, firmer start today
commentary.body: The ASX 200 slipped 0.5% on Friday to 9,020.8 but still gained 1.3% for the week. On Monday it dipped below 9,000 before closing 0.1% higher at 9,029.7: miners rose 2.9% (BHP, Lynas and James Hardie led), while the banks fell, with ANZ down 3.2% after its full-year result. Goodman Group gained 1.9% after confirming it and Digital Realty hold a 9.9% stake in NextDC. This morning the index opened 0.7% higher at about 9,093 following Wall Street, with gold near US$4,145 an ounce and firmer copper supporting miners while lower oil weighs on energy stocks.

commentary.heading: Rates: strong US jobs keep a Fed hike in play
commentary.body: The RBA's cash rate is 4.85% after last week's fifth hike of the year, with a pause widely expected at the 8 December meeting. In the US, the strong October jobs figures keep alive the chance the Fed lifts its 3.75–4.00% range on 9 December, although wages are growing only 3.1% a year, behind 3.7% inflation. US October inflation figures land overnight and will be the key test. The Bank of England sits at 4% after last week's hike.

commentary.heading: Bonds and the dollar
commentary.body: Australia's 10-year yield is around 5.03%, close to its lowest since August, and the US 10-year about 4.87%. UK 10-year gilt yields have eased to around 5.1%, also near their lowest since late August, as investors sought safety during the tech sell-off. The Australian dollar is steady at about 69.3 US cents.

commentary.heading: China and Hong Kong
commentary.body: China's inflation slowed to 0.7% in October (forecast 0.8%), with core inflation at 0.8%, as cheaper food offset a 22% jump in petrol prices. Factory-gate prices rose 5.7%, the fastest since June 2022, on energy costs, a widening gap that points to weak consumer demand. Beijing's State Council pledged on Friday to strengthen measures to stabilise the share market; the Shanghai Composite rose 0.3% on Monday to 3,661, while the Shenzhen Component and the Hang Seng (24,449) edged lower.

commentary.heading: What to watch
commentary.body: US October inflation (released early Wednesday morning, Sydney time) and US producer prices on Friday; whether the rebound in AI and chip stocks holds; developments at Nvidia; oil prices and US–Iran talks; China's loan prime rate on 20 November; and the RBA (8 December) and Fed (9 December) decisions.
